He said among the new facilities provided was a dedicated lactation room for breastfeeding mothers, in addition to improvements to the staff rest area to provide a more comfortable environment with greater privacy.

“In addition, the State Assembly Building Gallery has been rebranded as ‘Warisan Visual Terukir’ (Engraved Visual Heritage) to showcase the history and contributions of Penang State Assemblymen who have served from 1959 to 2026,” he said in a statement today.

He said the upgrading efforts also included the provision of a Special Officers’ Room equipped with workspaces, printing facilities and audio-visual equipment, as well as improvements to the State Assembly Meeting Room, which can now accommodate up to 25 people at any one time.
Law said the special media conference area had also been upgraded to provide greater comfort for media practitioners covering the assembly sitting.

The upgrading works will continue after the sitting concludes, including improvements to the disabled-friendly toilet near the guardhouse and the renovation of the general storeroom to ensure that equipment used during assembly sittings can be stored in a more orderly and organised manner. — Bernama
116a664aec224964: Royal London plans to cut hundreds of IT jobs and shift work to India under an outsourcing deal with IBM, according to sources, with redundancies expected by the end of December.

Sources said Royal London's chief technology officer, James Sandell, told IT staff in September that the insurance and pensions giant was partnering with IBM to outsource a substantial portion of its technology operations. A consultation process was expected to follow.

A Royal London spokesperson told The Register: "Royal London has appointed IBM as its strategic technology infrastructure partner as it continues to develop its technology strategy. The partnership will give Royal London access to IBM’s specialist capability, scale and experience. Royal London will remain accountable for service delivery and regulatory requirements and continues to focus on ensuring continuity and quality of service for customers."
We asked Royal London how many UK IT roles it would retain and whether IBM would move work to India.

The exact number of jobs at risk remains unclear, although one Glassdoor review posted on October 6 claims that hundreds of positions in the company's technology operations division are being eliminated.
"A vast amount of knowledge is being lost by the business, a lot that is not yet documented due to constant years of recruitment freeze and workload volume," they wrote.

The reviewer also questioned whether management had grasped just how much work would be involved in handing operations over to IBM, particularly with already stretched teams being cut to a fraction of their former size.
Royal London replied to the Glassdoor review, acknowledging staff concerns about the changes, though it didn't comment on the claims about outsourcing and redundancies.

"We recognise that as Royal London is going through a period of transformation, this has raised questions and concerns for some colleagues," the company wrote. "We have established channels for colleagues to raise these, including through People Leaders and Colleague Representatives, and I encourage colleagues to use these routes to discuss their concerns."
Other October reviews questioned the handling of the outsourcing and Royal London's commitment to its mutual values.
An October 12 reviewer identifying themselves as an IT infrastructure employee said the company had historically offered good career prospects, before criticizing its new direction.

"Sudden outsourcing goes against all Royal London values," the reviewer wrote, adding that employees were questioning the company's direction amid reports of a hiring freeze and further potential cuts.
Another review, posted on October 20, suggested the IBM deal was the latest in a series of outsourcing decisions following an earlier move to transfer servicing jobs to South Africa.
"A mutual company but not mutual values when it comes to things like this," the reviewer claimed.
The planned cuts follow rising profits. Royal London reported adjusted group operating profit of £187 million in the first half of 2026, up 13 percent year-on-year.

Royal London has been keen to trumpet the benefits of its mutual structure, under which it is owned by customers rather than shareholders. Reporting the results in August, chief executive Barry O'Dwyer highlighted the £199 million distributed to eligible customers through ProfitShare in April.
"As a customer-owned business, when we do well, our customers share in that success," O'Dwyer said.
For employees facing redundancy before Christmas, the benefits of that success may be somewhat harder to appreciate.
The Reg has asked IBM to comment. ®
0783ea4e5d2a5ff7: HANG TUAH JAYA: Kerajaan sedia mendedahkan kandungan perjanjian keyakinan dan perbekalan (CSA) yang dimeterai dengan sekumpulan Ahli Parlimen pembangkang susulan desakan PAS supaya butiran perjanjian itu diumumkan kepada umum, kata Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim.
Beliau berkata pihaknya tiada halangan untuk mendedahkan kandungan CSA berkenaan kerana prinsipnya sama seperti perjanjian yang pernah dimeterai antara kerajaan dan pembangkang sebelum ini.
Anwar berkata perkara itu akan dibangkitkan kepada Timbalan Perdana Menteri Fadillah Yusof, yang bertanggungjawab menguruskan perjanjian berkenaan, pada mesyuarat Jemaah Menteri esok.
"Saya tidak ada masalah, boleh dedahkan kerana prinsipnya sama seperti yang ditandatangani dulu.

"Esok dalam mesyuarat Jemaah Menteri, saya akan sampaikan perkara ini kepada Fadillah. Saya tidak ada keberatan untuk mendedahkannya," katanya selepas menghadiri Majlis Anugerah Tangan Emas Perdana Menteri 2026 di Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka (UTeM).

Beliau mengulas desakan Setiausaha Agung PAS Takiyuddin Hassan supaya kerajaan mendedahkan kandungan CSA, termasuk jumlah peruntukan pembangunan kawasan yang diterima Ahli Parlimen terlibat, kaedah penyaluran serta pelaksanaannya.

Terdahulu, Takiyuddin membangkitkan memorandum persefahaman (MoU) yang dimeterai antara kerajaan Ismail Sabri Yaakob dengan Pakatan Harapan (PH) pada 13 Sept 2021, yang menurutnya mengandungi prinsip tiada kerahsiaan dan didedahkan sepenuhnya kepada umum.
Ahli Parlimen Kota Bharu itu turut mempersoalkan mengapa kandungan CSA terbaharu belum diumumkan, sedangkan perjanjian terdahulu boleh diakses orang ramai.

Kerajaan pada 29 Okt lalu memeterai CSA dengan 13 Ahli Parlimen, terdiri daripada enam wakil Bersatu diketuai Muhyiddin Yassin, enam bekas wakil parti itu dan Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.
Perjanjian itu merangkumi sokongan terhadap Belanjawan 2027 serta reformasi institusi, dengan wakil rakyat terbabit menerima peruntukan pembangunan kawasan setara Ahli Parlimen kerajaan.
Mengulas kecaman Presiden PAS Hadi Awang yang menyifatkan CSA sebagai 'pendekatan dajal', Anwar berkata pemimpin itu sepatutnya lebih berhati-hati mengeluarkan kenyataan sebagai seorang agamawan.
"Sepatutnya kenyataan dia lebih terkawal. Itu tanggungjawab, bukan ditujukan kepada saya.
"Tetapi untuk menghukum orang atau kumpulan dengan pendirian dajal, itu tidak kena. Saya tidak fikir agama boleh dipermainkan seperti itu," katanya.
7f82568863b4327d: PETALING JAYA: A 21-year-old Muslim man who courted controversy for performing rituals associated with another faith has publicly declared his repentance alongside his mother and younger sister.
Aliff Daniel Adli, his mother Rohizayanti Ramli, 52, and his sister, Nur Ranea Ezreen Adli, 19, took part in the istitabah, or public declaration of repentance, Harian Metro reported.
The ceremony was organised by the Selangor Islamic religious department (Jais) at the Islamic lecture and discussion hall of Sultan Salahuddin Abdul Aziz Shah Mosque in Shah Alam.
This follows Aliff’s guilty plea yesterday at the Gombak Barat shariah lower court on a charge of deviant worship.
Judge Faizal Habib ordered Aliff to undergo three months of rehabilitation at Pusat Pemurnian Akidah Baitul Iman in Ulu Yam.

According to the charge, he committed deviant worship by holding up religious artefacts associated with another faith, performing rituals involving body piercing, and kneeling with both hands clasped against his chest in front of a statue at a temple in Batu Caves.
He committed the offence on Jan 24, 2024, between 9pm and 11pm.

The charge was framed under Section 4(1) of the Syariah Criminal Offences (Selangor) Enactment 1995, which provides for a fine of up to RM3,000, imprisonment for up to two years or both upon conviction.
f93c7b5e3bfabb1f: PARIS, Nov 5 — He has been behind some of Nintendo’s biggest hits, but producer Eiji Aonuma still feels “nervous” as he awaits players’ reactions to the new Zelda video game, Ocarina of Time out November 5.

“I’m all nervous about releasing the remake of ‘Ocarina’ because I don’t know how it’s going to turn out, I can’t stop thinking about it,” the 63-year-old Japanese creator, one of the most respected figures in video games, told AFP during a visit to Paris.
For over 25 years Aonuma has steered the series, which many people consider one of the best video games ever made.
Created in 1986 by Nintendo legend and Mario inventor Shigeru Miyamoto, who was Aonuma’s mentor, the series has enjoyed growing success.
Its last two main installments, Breath of the Wild (2017) and Tears of the Kingdom (2023), sold more than 55 million copies between them.
Islands in the sky
Poetic, melancholy and ground-breaking for its era, what set the original “Ocarina” apart was its sweeping story, shifting between the childhood and adulthood of its hero, Link.
Floating islands in the sky, a wind-swept ocean — The Legend of Zelda under Aonuma’s direction has evolved to offer ever vaster and more open worlds.
The series centres on the adventures of the green-clad warrior Link, who battles the evil demon Ganondorf across the ages trying to save Princess Zelda.
“I’ve worked a lot on using space to surprise players and spark their imagination,” said the designer, in order to “create games that instil in them the joy of exploration”.
Infusing the saga with this intrepid spirit is where the Japanese creator says he feels he has made his mark on the series.
It is “the very essence of Zelda today.”
Karakuri dolls and 3D
To keep players engaged, the Zelda saga alternates between major releases, smaller titles, side adventures and remakes of older titles.
Ocarina of Time is by far the most ambitious of its remakes, and its release is part of the 40th anniversary of the saga.
The new installment has a special meaning for Aonuma, the son of a telecommunications engineer and second of three children.
The original Ocarina of Time, released in 1998, was the first project he worked on with Miyamoto.
At university Aonuma studied design and in particular 3D composition through Karakuri dolls — traditional Japanese automatons.

A keen drawer, he joined Nintendo somewhat by chance in the late 1980s and worked as a graphic artist before being spotted by the Mario creator, who brought him onto the team working on the fifth Zelda game.
“It was the first time Nintendo was creating games in 3D,” he recalls.
He went on to take the helm of its sequel, Majora’s Mask (2000), and directed several installments before moving into a producer role to oversee the development of the saga.
Young blood
Some of the younger members of his team have never played the original Ocarina, bringing a freshness to the creative mix for the remake.

“It’s thanks to these young people, by thinking about how to adapt the game in the best possible way, how to make it fun once you have the controls in your hands, that this remake came into being,” he says.
On Friday in Paris, Aonuma was made Knight of the Order of Arts and Letters at the French culture ministry, an honour also bestowed two decades earlier on Miyamoto.
In his thank-you speech Aonuma said “the road travelled has not always been easy,” but he does not yet seem ready to pass the baton.

“I’m very interested to see what the younger staff will imagine” for future titles, he said, adding that he was “extremely happy” to offer his guidance so they can “think together” about the next Zelda. — AFP
9727c89834faf792: PUTRAJAYA: Bekas pensyarah kanan di Universiti Selangor (Unisel) menang rayuan terakhirnya selepas Mahkamah Rayuan memutuskan beliau dipecat secara terancang susulan penurunan pangkat dan pemotongan gaji atas dakwaan salah laku.

Dalam keputusan majoriti 2-1, Mahkamah Rayuan memutuskan tindakan berterusan Pendidikan Industri YS Sdn Bhd, iaitu syarikat yang mengendalikan universiti itu, merupakan pelanggaran asas terhadap kontrak perkhidmatan Siti Asmahan Ali.
Hakim Faizah Jamaludin, yang menyampaikan penghakiman majoriti, berkata Siti Asmahan berjaya memenuhi beban undang-undang membuktikan beliau dipecat secara terancang.
Hakim Ahmad Shahrir Mohd Salleh sependapat dengan keputusan berkenaan, manakala Radzi Abdul Hamid menentang.
Mahkamah Rayuan mengetepikan keputusan Mahkamah Perusahaan dan Mahkamah Tinggi, lalu mengisytiharkan Siti Asmahan dipecat secara terancang, tanpa sebab atau alasan adil.

Kes itu dihantar semula ke Mahkamah Perusahaan untuk menentukan jumlah ganti rugi yang patut diterima Siti Asmahan, termasuk tunggakan gaji dan pampasan sebagai ganti pemulihan jawatan. Justeru, Mahkamah Rayuan telah menyelesaikan isu liabiliti, dan hanya meninggalkan penilaian remedi untuk ditentukan.
Siti Asmahan menyertai Unisel pada 2001 sebagai pensyarah di Fakulti Pengurusan Industri dan dinaikkan pangkat pensyarah kanan, pada 2007.
Selepas berkhidmat hampir 20 tahun, beliau berdepan siasatan dalaman pada akhir tahun 2020 berikutan satu mesej dimuat naik dalam kumpulan WhatsApp tidak rasmi kakitangan.

Panel siasatan mendapati pertuduhan terhadapnya terbukti dan bertindak menurunkan pangkatnya daripada pensyarah kanan kepada pensyarah (Gred DS45), berserta pemotongan gaji. Rayuan dalamannya terhadap hukuman tersebut turut ditolak.
Bekas pensyarah dituduh
Siti Asmahan mendakwa proses tatatertib tersebut tidak adil dan tindakan menunjukkan pihak universiti tidak lagi berniat mematuhi terma kontrak perkhidmatannya.
Antara lain, beliau mengadu lima saksi memberi keterangan terhadapnya tanpa kehadirannya, dan beliau tidak diberi peluang yang bermakna mengemukakan kesnya dalam rayuan dalaman.
Beliau turut mengadu individu sama yang mengenakan hukuman tersebut terlibat dalam membuat keputusan bagi rayuannya.
Oleh itu, beliau menganggap dirinya telah dipecat secara terancang dan mengemukakan representasi mengikut Seksyen 20 Akta Perhubungan Perusahaan 1967.
Dapatan mahkamah
Dalam membenarkan rayuannya, Faizah berkata tindakan majikan mestilah dinilai secara objektif dan kumulatif, bukannya meneliti setiap insiden secara berasingan.
Beliau berkata, panel tatatertib membentuk sebahagian daripada majikan dan menjalankan kuasa membuat keputusan bagi pihak syarikat.

Walaupun universiti berhak menurunkan pangkatnya, hukuman dikenakan mestilah setimpal. Hukuman dikenakan adalah berat, memandangkan ia menekan kedudukan akademik kanannya selain berdepan pengurangan gaji.
Keputusan majoriti itu juga mendapati beliau berulang kali diarah berdiam diri semasa proses tatatertib, selain rayuan dalaman tidak memberinya peluang bermakna untuk didengari.

Panel hakim menolak hujah majikan bahawa sebarang kelemahan dalam siasatan dalaman dan rayuan dalaman telah diperbaiki apabila Mahkamah Perusahaan mendengar semula dakwaan salah laku berkenaan dari awal.

Mereka berkata, Mahkamah Perusahaan gagal mempertimbangkan kesan kumulatif daripada tindakan majikan menentukan sama ada berlaku pelanggaran asas terhadap kontrak perkhidmatan. Mahkamah Tinggi juga membuat kesilapan sama.
Pihak syarikat tersebut turut diperintah membayar kos RM50,000.
Siti Asmahan diwakili Simrenjeet Singh dan Nicholas Ng, manakala Nor Aziah Harun, Nurfarah Athirah Faizal Tan, dan Arif Kamil Abdul Rahman Kamil bertindak bagi pihak syarikat.

6c044d14d7a94e7c: TOKYO: Japanese gaming giant Nintendo reported a drop in quarterly net profit on Thursday as unit sales slowed for its Switch 2 console, but maintained its annual forecasts.
A remake of 1990s action-adventure classic "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time", which comes out Thursday, has sparked nostalgic fan excitement.
But market analysts will be watching to see how much the title can boost sales of the Switch 2, which became the world's fastest-selling games console on its 2025 release.
Nintendo reported an 11% year-on-year rise in net profit for the first half of 2026-27.
But in the second quarter, from July-September, net profit was down 29% to 73.5 billion yen (US$465.3 million) -- missing estimates of 82.2 billion yen in a Bloomberg survey of analysts.
The company maintained its annual net profit forecast of 310 billion yen.

6b2c477ddc456132: NOVEMBER 5 — Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing the way we seek and receive information, including information about our health. Today, many people use AI-powered applications to ask questions about symptoms, interpret medical reports and understand possible health conditions. Some even upload photographs of skin problems, dental conditions or medical images to obtain an instant assessment. Although this technology offers exciting possibilities, we need to pause and ask an important question: Can we really trust AI to diagnose our medical and dental conditions?

There is no doubt that AI has the potential to improve healthcare. It can analyse large amounts of information, recognise patterns and assist healthcare professionals in interpreting medical images. In medicine, AI systems are being developed to help detect abnormalities in X-rays, CT scans and other diagnostic images. In dentistry, AI can assist in identifying possible tooth decay, bone loss associated with gum disease and other abnormalities in dental X-rays. For example, an AI system may highlight an area on a dental X-ray that could indicate tooth decay, helping a dentist identify areas that require closer examination. When used appropriately, these tools may improve efficiency, support clinical decision-making and contribute to earlier detection of certain conditions.

However, there is another side to the story. AI is not a doctor or dentist, and it can get things wrong. An AI application may provide an answer that sounds confident and convincing but is inaccurate or incomplete. Consider someone experiencing severe toothache. After uploading a photograph, an AI application suggests that the problem is simply tooth decay. However, the actual cause could be a dental abscess, a cracked tooth or an infection involving the surrounding tissues. These conditions may require further investigations and different treatments. If the person relies entirely on the AI-generated answer, they may delay seeking proper dental care, potentially allowing the condition to worsen.

Another important point to remember is that AI does not always provide the same answer to every question. Different AI applications may generate different responses, even when given the same symptoms or photographs. Sometimes, the answer may also change depending on how the question is asked. This is because AI generates responses based on patterns in the information it has learned, rather than examining a patient in the same way a healthcare professional would. Therefore, receiving a consistent or convincing answer does not necessarily mean that the information is correct.

Why does this happen? A proper medical or dental diagnosis involves much more than looking at a photograph or prompting a list of symptoms. Doctors and dentists consider the patient’s medical history, conduct clinical examinations and, when necessary, request additional investigations before deciding on the most appropriate diagnosis and treatment. AI may not have access to all this information and cannot replace the professional judgement and clinical experience required to assess each individual patient.
Always verify information through reliable health sources and consult a qualified doctor or dentist for professional assessment and treatment. — Unsplash pic

Furthermore, every patient is different. Two people may have similar symptoms but completely different underlying conditions. For example, a white patch in the mouth may be caused by something harmless, such as irritation, but it could also be associated with an infection or a potentially serious oral condition. A dentist needs to consider factors such as the patient’s age, medical history, habits, duration of the lesion and clinical appearance before reaching a diagnosis. A photograph alone may not provide enough information to distinguish between these conditions.

Another issue that deserves attention is personal privacy. When using AI applications, people may upload medical reports, dental X-rays, photographs and other sensitive health information without fully understanding how their data will be collected, stored or used. Before sharing such information, users should check the platform’s privacy policies and avoid uploading identifiable personal or medical details unnecessarily. We should also be cautious about following treatment recommendations generated by AI. For instance, someone experiencing toothache may be advised to take certain medications or try home remedies based on the symptoms provided. However, not all medications are suitable for everyone, and some conditions require urgent treatment rather than temporary relief. Taking medication without proper advice or delaying treatment because an AI application suggests that the condition is not serious may put one’s health at risk. AI can provide general information, but decisions about medication and treatment should always be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

Does this mean we should avoid using AI for health information? Not at all! AI can be a useful starting point for understanding unfamiliar medical terms, learning about general health conditions and preparing questions before visiting a healthcare professional. We should also learn to use AI appropriately by asking questions that help us understand health information rather than seeking a diagnosis. For example, we can use AI to explain medical terms, understand common symptoms or prepare questions for our dentist. The important thing is to use it wisely. Treat AI-generated responses as general information rather than a confirmed diagnosis. Always verify information through reliable health sources and consult a qualified doctor or dentist for professional assessment and treatment. Most importantly, persistent pain, swelling, bleeding, fever or other concerning symptoms deserve professional attention.

As AI becomes increasingly accessible, it is important for the public to develop the ability to use this technology responsibly. It can be a helpful assistant, but it should never become our sole healthcare adviser. After all, your health is too important to leave to an algorithm. When in doubt, consult your doctor or dentist. Let AI inform you but let healthcare professionals care for you.

* The authors are Assoc Prof. Dr. Nor Azlida Binti Mohd Nor from the Department of Community Oral Health & Clinical Prevention, Faculty of Dentistry, Universiti Malaya, and Assoc. Prof. Dr. Goh Yet Ching from the Department of Oral & Maxillofacial Clinical Sciences, Faculty of Dentistry, Universiti Malaya.

In a statement, the central bank said the latest indicators pointed to continued resilience in global growth, supported by strong global technology investment and stable labour markets.
“At the current OPR level, the MPC considers the monetary policy stance to be consistent with the outlook of continued price stability and sustainable economic growth,” it said.
BNM said the MPC would remain vigilant to evolving conditions and assess their implications for the balance of risks surrounding the outlook for domestic inflation and economic growth.
Year-to-date, headline and core inflation averaged 1.8 per cent and 1.9 per cent, respectively, the central bank said.
Looking ahead to 2027, geopolitical developments, elevated global commodity prices and adverse weather conditions are expected to exert upward pressure on inflation.
Both headline and core inflation are therefore expected to edge higher, although they are likely to remain contained amid continued domestic policy measures and stable demand conditions.
“The MPC will remain vigilant to cost pressures and domestic demand conditions given their impact on the inflation outlook,” BNM said.
Inflation has edged higher following an increase in energy costs and is expected to remain elevated as higher costs continue to be passed through to consumer prices.

On the global outlook, BNM said uncertainties surrounding geopolitical developments would continue to weigh on growth and fuel inflationary pressures. However, the impact is expected to be cushioned by sustained technology-related spending and continued adaptation to supply constraints.

Downside risks to global growth include prolonged geopolitical tensions, tighter global financial conditions arising from monetary policy adjustments, concerns over financial market valuations and fiscal vulnerabilities.
“Upside potential could come from stronger technology spending and a faster-than-expected recovery in supply chain conditions,” the central bank said.
On the domestic front, recent indicators point to continued strength in economic growth in the third quarter of 2026, underpinned by robust exports and sustained domestic demand.
The solid momentum is expected to lift full-year growth in 2026 to above five per cent.
“Looking ahead, the economy’s sound fundamentals are expected to keep growth resilient in 2027.
“The external sector is expected to remain a major driver of growth, supported by the ongoing global technology upcycle and firm tourist spending,” BNM said.
Stable labour market conditions and continued investment activity are also expected to support domestic demand, while measures under Budget 2027 will provide further impetus to private consumption.
However, the growth outlook remains subject to downside risks, including a prolonged conflict in the Middle East and lower commodity production.
On the upside, stronger-than-expected global growth, firmer technology-related export demand and higher tourism activity could provide additional support to economic expansion, BNM added. — Bernama

22b3559c44474108: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 5 — Malaysia stood out in Southeast Asia’s initial public offering (IPO) market in the first nine months of 2026, accounting for 38 of the 56 listings recorded across the region, according to Ernst & Young (EY).

The 38 IPOs raised US$1.62 billion (RM6.56 billion, based on US$1=RM4.05), compared with US$992 million (RM4.02 billion) raised through 37 listings in the corresponding period last year, stated EY in a factsheet today.

In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q 2026), Malaysia recorded nine IPOs raising US$167.2 million (RM677.2 million), compared with eight IPOs that raised US$94 million (RM380.7 million) in the same quarter last year.

Among other Southeast Asian markets, Singapore recorded eight IPOs raising US$1.28 billion (RM5.18 billion), followed by Indonesia with seven IPOs raising US$121.3 million (RM491.3 million) and Thailand with three IPOs raising US$21.3 million (RM86.3 million).
Southeast Asia recorded 56 IPOs raising US$3 billion (RM12.15 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, a decline of 26 per cent in volume and 13 per cent in value year-on-year.
In 3Q 2026, 20 IPOs raised US$500 million (RM2.03 billion), compared with 26 IPOs that raised US$2.1 billion (RM8.51 billion) over the same period in 2025.
EY Capital Markets representative Nghia Trung Nguyen said Malaysia exceeded both the number of listings and proceeds recorded over the same period last year.
“The stronger proceeds are encouraging and point to continued investor appetite for quality companies with compelling growth prospects.

“This momentum also reflects the role of the capital market in supporting companies as they pursue their next phase of growth, providing access to capital while broadening their investor base and market profile,” he said in a statement.
Nghia said issuers needed to be well-prepared and realistic about market timing and investor expectations amid an uncertain global environment, as investors became increasingly selective.

He added that a compelling business proposition, supported by strong fundamentals, good governance and a clear growth strategy, remained crucial to securing a successful listing and sustaining investor confidence beyond the IPO.

EY Asean IPO leader Chan Yew Kiang said regulatory reforms, a muted economic outlook and geopolitical uncertainties had dampened listing sentiment across the region, prompting IPO aspirants to adopt a more cautious approach.

“Hence, in 3Q 2026, except Malaysia, IPO transaction counts across Southeast Asia slowed compared with the same period last year. Exchanges in the region also began to focus on unlocking shareholders’ value through different initiatives.

“For example, in Singapore, while the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP) that was introduced in February 2025 had injected liquidity and vibrancy into the local exchanges, more needs to be done by corporates to improve liquidity and post-IPO performance,” he said.

Globally, EY said there were 908 IPOs that raised US$290 billion (RM1.17 trillion) in the first nine months of 2026, representing a two per cent decline in deal volume but a 153 per cent increase in proceeds compared with the corresponding period in 2025.
It said for 3Q 2026, there were 387 IPOs that raised US$95.6 billion (RM387.2 billion), compared with 374 IPOs that raised US$52 billion (RM210.6 billion) over the same period in 2025.

In terms of regional performance, EY said Asia-Pacific recorded 399 IPOs raising US$93.2 billion (RM377.5 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 14 per cent in volume and 79 per cent in proceeds year-on-year.

Meanwhile, the Europe, Middle East, India and Africa (EMEIA) region recorded 389 IPOs raising US$30.2 billion (RM122.3 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, representing a one per cent increase in volume and six per cent in proceeds year-on-year.

According to EY, Americas’ IPO activity saw a 35 per cent decline in deal volume to 120 listings in the first nine months of 2026, although proceeds surged 392 per cent to US$166.6 billion (RM674.7 billion). — Bernama

669a0c8f4c667cce: Google Cloud has revealed that the cause of the October 20 outage in its europe-west-2-b availability zone was a ‘misconfiguration’ of its systems that meant its emergency generators didn’t start.
The outage at the London facility caused service interruptions at outfits including Lloyds, HSBC, Royal Mail, and Revolut.
In a November 4 update to its service status page, Google explained what went wrong.

“The site relies on a 2N utility power architecture — where the facility has complete duplicate power paths for every critical load — backed by a central high-voltage generator bank managed by a dual-redundant Programmable Logic Controller (PLC),” Google revealed.

The facility gets its juice from two independent utility feeders, which Google calls “A” and “B”. There’s also a “standby utility connection configured for manual campus-wide transfer during maintenance operations or emergency events.”
Google says the root cause of the incident was failure in an external underground cable through which its power supplier brings ‘leccy to its bit barns.
That cable connects to primary feeder A and it broke at a time when feeder B wasn’t working.

“Circuit breaker feeder B was physically opened to allow for corrective repairs following issues identified during a quarterly generator load test on 14 Oct 2026,” Google admitted. “Consequently, primary utility feed A was supporting the total critical load while the feed B breaker remained in an open position to allow repairs to be conducted on the B feeder pathway.”
That shouldn’t be a problem for a top-tier operator like Google, which knows it needs to install backup sources of electricity like uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and on-site generators.
Indeed, europe-west-2-b employs UPSes that Google says can keep things up and running for five minutes if the availability zone loses its connection to the grid.
The UPSes worked, but a “voltage-sensing design flaw and PLC misconfiguration prevented the facility’s generator plant from receiving an automatic start signal to assume the critical load.”
Google’s UPSes therefore ran out of juice, but its generators didn’t start. The rest is history.
The search giant has figured out that its PLCs weren’t set up to handle the conditions it faced on this fateful day.

“PLC logic indicated that a healthy utility source was available, even though the primary and secondary distribution feeds were de-energized, and did not issue a start command to the generator plant,” the status update reveals.
Once Google was able to reconnect to its power utility, it reprogrammed the PLC so it wouldn’t make the same mistake again.
The Big G has since made many changes to the electrical setup at europe-west-2-b and says it’s tested them and that they all work.

It’s also given itself two action items, one of which it describes as a “Communications Enhancement” that will see it “bolster notification speed by developing an automated alert-to-communication mechanism for location-impacting incidents.”
The other is to “expand platform-wide testing outcomes for infrastructure-level events.”
Once Google gets that done, perhaps it will be able to handle outages better – and if not, at least advise customers about its troubles more quickly. ®
cf403874a276142d: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013. Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths. Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment. It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.

The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning. The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.” It suggests something left behind, something unused. In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties. The label was not just a description of marital status. It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.

But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did. Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.

While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain. The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed. Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms. For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift. The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations. Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.

On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university. By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market. At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.

Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance. Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain. “Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.

Other posts question the pressure itself. One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.” (催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

Some women have even embraced and reclaimed the characterization of shengnü as a form of empowerment. Online, some social media posts explicitly recast the label through a play on Chinese characters: 剩, meaning “leftover,” becomes 胜, meaning “victorious,” with the same pronunciation, shèng. A Xiaohongshu post shared by an account named “Kevin” declares: “I’m not a ‘leftover woman’; I’m a ‘victorious woman.’” It advocates remaining single rather than settling, pursuing personal growth, and enjoying time alone.

In another post, the creator “小李存钱记” addresses her mother’s worries about her being unmarried at 30. “I’m not a leftover woman! I’m a victorious woman!” reads the text across the image. She describes juggling several jobs and building an online following, presenting her work and earnings as evidence of her worth. The reframing rejects marriage as the measure of success, while placing considerable emphasis on professional achievement and financial independence.

These posts do not erase the social stigma of the term shengnü. Rather, they show how users are challenging the label by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or replacing “leftover” with “victorious.” Yet the language of victory raises another question. If an unmarried woman must point to her earnings, career, or independence to defend her choices, how much room is there simply to be single?

e8bf6269fd8b236d: Anna Moneymaker/Getty The Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections puts them in a stronger position to interfere with President Donald Trump’s agenda. This includes his deeply unpopular and costly war against Iran, which could be among their first priorities. As president, Trump will be able to veto any legislation aimed at ending the war. But the Democrats still have another powerful card up their sleeves: cutting off funding for the war. There are caveats, however. History suggests exercising this power could trigger a political confrontation that may backfire. And even if the Democrats succeed in ending the war, they may not be able to reverse the damage it has done to the US’ global standing. The limits of legislation Democrats will have three main options to try to force the war against Iran to a close. Two of these, however, face significant limitations. The first – and perhaps most obvious – option is through legislation. There are a few different ways to do this. One approach is to pass a resolution calling for an end to the war. Congress already attempted this in June, passing a concurrent resolution (with the support of some Republicans) that directed the president to either withdraw US forces from hostilities against Iran or seek the approval of Congress before continuing. This was done under the War Powers Resolution of 1973. These so-called concurrent resolutions are, however, widely seen as non-binding. Intended to express the opinion or will of Congress, they are generally used to deal with internal matters within Congress. Trump ignored it. A similar resolution then failed in the Senate in September. For such a resolution to be binding, it would need the force of a law passed by Congress, which the president would likely veto. To overcome that veto, the Democrats would need the support of a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate. This would require a significant number of Republicans to cross the aisle. Exercising oversight A second option for the Democrats is to launch a series of congressional investigations into the way the war has been conducted. This would likely include public hearings, subpoenas and demands for documents from the Trump administration. The Democrats may also attempt to impeach senior officials in the Trump administration. If Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat tipped to become the next speaker of the House, wants to appease some of the more progressive voices in his party – or the hardline voices on the Iran war or against Trump – Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be targeted for impeachment. But the grounds for such proceedings are unclear at this stage, and even with the Democrats’ new Senate majority, he would be unlikely to be convicted unless a significant number of Republicans crossed the aisle. More pertinently, congressional investigations are a protracted process, and unlikely to bring the war to a swift end. The ‘power of the purse’ The more immediate power that Congress has to end the war swiftly is in Article I, Section 9 of the US Constitution, which states: No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law […] This is known as the “power of the purse”. Once the new Congress is sworn in in January, every new dollar that Trump’s Department of War wants to spend needs to be approved by the House and the Senate. A Democrat-controlled Congress could put a clause into the defence budget, prohibiting funds from being used for hostilities against Iran. Trump could veto this, but this would mean blocking the paycheck for everyone in the military, as well. The Democrats tried this very approach in 2007, attempting to force a timetable for a US withdrawal from Iraq. Then-President George W. Bush vetoed it, but it became a political football, with both sides accusing the other of leaving US troops unfunded. The Democrats ultimately backed down due to the growing risk of backlash from voters. Today, this approach would carry a similar risk. Are the Democrats willing to put their political credibility on the line if the president accuses them of letting American soldiers down? Who blinks first? Republicans face a reckoning As the dust settled on Wednesday, Trump himself acknowledged the Iran war had played a role in the Republican Party’s crushing defeat. But he doubled down on the decision, saying he would do it all over again if necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. Vice President JD Vance was less defensive. In a detailed statement posted to X, Vance bluntly declared the war was the reason the Republicans lost. He added, “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there”. Vance has long criticised US military involvement in overseas conflicts, but in his role as vice president has publicly backed Trump’s actions against Iran. This week’s overwhelming Democratic victory has made it much easier for Vance – and other Republicans – to now break ranks with the president. The balance of power has shifted For Trump, bringing the war to an end now would mean humiliation. The US has so far poured almost US$50 billion into a military campaign with few tangible achievements. On top of that, Iran has learned that the Strait of Hormuz is a chokepoint it can control. The same is true for the Bab al-Mandeb Strait off the coast of Yemen, where the Iran-aligned Houthis have attacked commercial ships. These costs will outlast the Trump presidency. The war might definitively bring to an end the unipolar global order Washington built after the end of the Cold War. The biggest winner may not be Tehran, but Beijing. d844d9cf680182a6: We were promised a panacea for the climate crisis and a way to save our food system. So why is nobody firing up the chicken vats? Not just any burger: a world-historic burger, made from cattle cells grown in a laboratory by Mark Post, a professor of vascular physiology at Maastricht University in the Netherlands. Now it was being tasted in public for the first time at Riverside Studios in London, at an event attended by 200 members of the press and livestreamed to thousands. To make this particular burger, Post had extracted stem cells from the shoulder muscle of a living cow, then cultivated them in plastic containers filled with a nutrient-rich supplement called foetal bovine serum, which is derived from cow foetuses. The cells eventually became 20,000 strands of tissue, which in turn became a single 140g patty. Post believed that beef produced this way had the potential to dramatically reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and slow the climate crisis. Raising cattle for consumption requires massive amounts of land and water – and massive amounts of feed grown at a high environmental cost. He projected that global demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it the old-fashioned way, at which point our food systems would become unsustainable. 16de4ca3c25d3eed: In an emergency, a human might someday ask a robotic assistant to fetch a wall-mounted defibrillator located down the hall. But if the robot has incorrectly labeled the defibrillator as a fire extinguisher in its stored memory, it may not know where to find the life-saving device. This robotic assistant could benefit from a new memory system created by MIT researchers. The system identifies entries in a robot’s memory that might be wrong and corrects the descriptions of mislabeled objects.  In the future, this method could make household or industrial robots better able to perform complex, multistep tasks, such as clearing a dining room table or working alongside human collaborators to assemble a piece of machinery.  Called UQ-DAAAM (which stands for Uncertainty Quantification for Describe Anything, Anywhere, at Any Moment), the system compares multiple descriptions of the same object, seen from different viewpoints, to quantify the robot’s uncertainty about what it saw.  It then selects additional views to reduce the uncertainty and combines these captions into a more accurate description of the object, which it saves to memory. The researchers also employed a special technique to streamline this process so a mobile robot can continually update uncertain memory entries in real time.  When compared to baseline methods, UQ-DAAAM boosted the robot’s confidence and improved the accuracy of its answers to questions about objects, their locations, and when it saw them.  “Contrary to ChatGPT, when we think about physical AI, it is not enough to simply put a disclaimer cautioning that sometimes the robot might be wrong. Allowing a robot to know what it doesn’t know is going to be essential for this technology to be deployed safely and have a positive impact on society,” says Luca Carlone, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro), principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), director of the MIT SPARK Laboratory, and the senior author of the paper presenting UQ-DAAAM. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Harry Zhang and Nicolas Gorlo. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.  Amending memory This new method builds on the researchers’ prior work, DAAAM, a robot memory system that uses a vision-language model (VLM) to richly describe objects in scenes a robot captures with its onboard cameras. These descriptions are stored as detailed captions in a 3D map-based representation of the robot’s environment that it can call upon later to answer questions.  But the robot sometimes sees objects only partially or from far away, or its camera might capture blurry or poorly lit images. In these cases, DAAAM might describe these objects incorrectly, such as by mistaking a gray chimney for a squirrel perched on a rooftop. “With no way to correct itself, this wrong memory would persist as the robot proceeds in its environment, which could impact downstream applications,” Zhang says. UQ-DAAAM integrates uncertainty quantification into the DAAAM framework. It allows the robot to measure its confidence in the accuracy of object descriptions and fix incorrect captions as it travels through an environment. While on the move, the robot constantly collects and stores images of the world around it. Many of these images show the same objects captured from different angles. UQ-DAAAM uses these additional viewpoints to identify and correct unreliable descriptions. First, it calculates the VLM’s confidence level in the words it generated to describe a potentially mislabeled object. Then, it measures consistency by comparing this description to captions of images that describe the same object from different vantage points. “We fuse both sources of uncertainty into a single number that captures how certain the VLM is in its overall understanding of the object,” Carlone explains. If that number exceeds a certain threshold, the uncertainty is too high, and UQ-DAAAM will refine the caption by using additional images of the object. It does this using a heuristic, or simple rule, that determines which additional viewpoints will reduce the robot’s uncertainty about the object. For instance, it might choose an image captured a few frames later that clearly shows smoke emanating from the chimney.  The researchers mathematically proved that this heuristic can identify the best frames to select without rerunning the VLM, dramatically reducing the amount of computation.  “The key challenge Nico and Harry had to overcome is how to combine VLMs with uncertainty quantification into something that is running in a fraction of a second on a robot that is moving,” Carlone says. Remembering with confidence Once it has identified additional captions that will reduce its uncertainty about the object, the system uses an LLM to fuse them into a single object description. To boost accuracy, the LLM puts more weight on new captions and those with less ambiguity. This refinement step is able to resolve ambiguities for about 92 percent of the objects in the robot’s environment, while only requiring two additional captions per object. It increased the accuracy of object descriptions by 5 percent compared to the state of the art. UQ-DAAAM also provided more accurate answers to questions about the objects it observed, where it saw them, and when it last encountered them than baseline methods. “Performing this uncertainty quantification procedure across the entire map the robot generates allows it to improve its understanding of what it has observed,” Gorlo says. Next, the researchers want to use UQ-DAAAM to guide different types of robots, like mobile robotic manipulators, and apply their uncertainty quantification techniques to other domains.  In addition, they are studying the use of UQ-DAAAM to identify areas of high uncertainty the robot could revisit to improve its understanding of the environment. They are also exploring uncertainty quantification in systems that predict the future state of a robot’s environment. This research is supported, in part, by the U.S. Army Research Laboratory and the U.S. Office of Naval Research. Carlone is currently on sabbatical as an Amazon Scholar; this article describes work performed at MIT and is not associated with Amazon.

2e0612d18143103c: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.
449e386054c8faa3: VMware appears to have made a concession to European regulators by extending the life of its low-end vSphere Standard and Enterprise Plus products.
The virtualization pioneer quietly announced the extension in the November 4 blog post in which it announced a new low-end product called vSphere Express, which The Register reported yesterday.
We based our report about vSphere Express on an interview, and on material provided by VMware – which sent a version of the blog post linked to above.
The version we saw did not include the following paragraph, the contents of which were not mentioned in our interview:

“Furthermore, for customers in countries in the European Economic Area, vSphere Standard version 8 and vSphere Enterprise Plus version 8 will remain available for sale until October 31, 2027, and will have Extended Support included in any active subscriptions to those offerings until the earlier of the applicable subscription end date or October 31, 2028.”
The latter date is more than a year past the October 11, 2027, end-of-general-support date for the more capable vSphere 8 and Cloud Foundation 5.x products.

“This has the potential to be a positive development for organisations within the European Economic Area,” independent analyst Michael Warrilow told The Register. “It could provide them up to an extra 12 months to transition vSphere 8 to VCF 9 and/or migrate workloads to another platform.”
Warrilow thinks European users should seek “absolute clarity” from VMware about the specifics of its offer.
“What level of extended support will be provided and what longer-term commitments will need to be made? I cannot find any of that detail,” he wrote.

A reminder: VMware has promised in the past to make patches available for users who choose to persist with perpetual licenses instead of moving to its preferred subscriptions. The Broadcom business unit later paused patch downloads for months, claiming it needed to adjust its website to make them possible.
Warrilow wonders why VMware will keep selling vSphere Standard only in Europe and suggested “regulatory muscle” is the reason.
Regulators around the world cleared Broadcom’s acquisition of VMware. In Europe, authorities have since revisited the matter.

Lobby group Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe (CISPE) has succeeded in having the European Commission open an antitrust investigation into whether VMware’s channel changes inappropriately shaped the cloud infrastructure provider market. The Register understands CISPE feels regulators are receptive to its arguments.
In the Netherlands, local courts enforced a VMware support contract of the sort that Broadcom has tried to walk away from at other users.
Warrilow wonders if VMware might now change its policy regarding vSphere Standard in other countries.

“The subsequent question is how can organisations in other regions get the same concessions from Broadcom? I would encourage them to amplify their voice by rallying industry associations and user groups to the cause whilst lobbying the regulators in their jurisdiction.”
Overall, however, he thinks VMware’s decision isn’t enormously impactful.
“Ultimately, all it does is buy a little more time to upgrade or migrate,” he wrote.
It may not even do that, as The Register often heard that VMware seldom issued quotes for vSphere Standard or Enterprise Plus.
Paul Turner, chief product officer for VMware’s Cloud Foundation Division, told The Register that inappropriate incentives for channel partners caused that situation, and that VMware later fixed it.
Continental users will be hoping VMware got that effort right. ®

b9b4a6a49c564e9c: When The Register writes about professional certifications offered by vendors, we often receive comments arguing that such credentials are nowhere near as valuable as real-world experience. Now, Microsoft has acknowledged there’s some merit in that argument.

Redmond revealed its stance last week in a post from general manager for content and insights Cameron Percy, who observed: “For years, people have asked for a simpler way to prove the skills they use in the flow of work, without stepping away to prepare for another test.”
Microsoft’s response is the “Pro Badge,” a new form of credential that Percy wrote “works alongside Microsoft Certifications.”

“Certifications show that you can solve problems in a role or field. Pro Badge shows how you use a specific product in your everyday work. Together, they give a more complete picture of what you can do.”

“Instead of capturing skills on a single test day, this approach keeps pace with your work and the products you use,” Percy added. “It gives you a current, verified signal of what you can do, at no cost and without a separate exam or study guide.”
The first Pro Badge is for GitHub Copilot. To earn it, users need only visit learn.github.com and sign in with their GitHub account.

Going through those steps fires up a “proficiency engine” that Microsoft says “gets to work analyzing relevant product usage signals and evaluating them against a defined proficiency framework.” Percy’s post says it “systematically uses evidence from everyday product use to calculate and automatically update your proficiency level.”
Microsoft offers five levels of proficiency: beginner, intermediate, proficient, advanced, and expert. To earn a Pro Badge, users must reach the proficient level.
A beginner has had “first contact” with GitHub and “understands what Copilot is, where it can be used, and how it might fit into everyday development workflows.”
An intermediate user is “familiar with web-based collaboration features, core IDE features, model management, agent configuration, customization options, and techniques for managing context.”

To score the Pro Badge, users will need to demonstrate “practical ability to work on projects” and use GitHub “across typical scenarios, demonstrated through consistent hands-on usage across multiple repositories and extended periods.”

“A Proficient user can use many web and IDE features, select appropriate models, and apply customizations to tailor Copilot for specific project needs. They have experimented with extended features and are aware of extensibility/integration options.”
At the time of writing, Redmond hasn’t defined expert or advanced proficiency. It has published more criteria for the first three levels here.
Microsoft has kindly integrated GitHub’s learning site with LinkedIn, which it owns, so users can add Pro Badges to their profiles.
Percy’s post suggests Microsoft has other Pro Badges in the works.
Elsewhere, Microsoft makes it plain that Pro Badges won’t replace its other credentials.

“GitHub Verified Proficiency is part of Microsoft Pro Badge, a new credential type designed to recognize skills as they are applied in the flow of work,” explains a page offering detail of the new cred. “It does not replace certifications or Microsoft Applied Skills. It adds a third signal: how skills show up through everyday product use.”
The Register welcomes comment on this new approach to professional credentials. ®

9e4e5c2c7d2c59f6: BANGKOK: A benchmark Asian rice price climbed to the highest in almost two years, threatening to accelerate food inflation as the El Nino weather pattern disrupts production of the staple grain.

Farmers across much of Asia are in the midst of harvesting the grain, and drier-than-usual weather has proven a hurdle for crops in growers like India, the world’s leading exporter. Global production is expected to decline this season for the first time in over a decade, the US agriculture department forecasts.

That’s pushing prices higher, with 5% broken white rice from Thailand -- another major shipper -- rising to US$499 a tonne as of Wednesday, the highest since December 2024, according to the Thai Rice Exporters Association. Rough rice futures in Chicago are also up more than 80% since the start of the year.

Those gains come even as prices decline for other major grains, including corn and wheat. The El Nino weather phenomenon underway is one of the most powerful on record and linked to drier conditions across much of South and Southeast Asia, where more than half the world’s rice is grown.
In Thailand, the main production risk is for the off-season crop, which relies on irrigation, the USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service said in a recent report.

While higher wholesale prices take time to feed through to retail markets, there are already signs of rising costs in some places. Rice prices in the Philippines, the No. 1 importer, jumped 21% in October versus a year earlier, according to government figures released Thursday.
The grain is a dietary staple across swathes of Asia, Africa and the Middle East. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization also expects a drop in world output during the 2026-27 season.

b307ab9ce0727765: KUALA LUMPUR: Will Bank Negara Malaysia raise interest rates today? And if it does, how much more could you end up paying on your housing loan?
The central bank will announce its final interest rate decision of the year at 3pm, with most economists expecting it to keep the overnight policy rate (OPR) unchanged at 2.75 per cent.
However, some believe stronger economic growth has strengthened the case for raising the OPR to three per cent, effectively reversing the pre-emptive cut made in July 2025.
Bank Negara lowered the OPR by 25 basis points last year to cushion the economy against global uncertainties, particularly US trade tariffs.
But Malaysia's economy has since performed better than expected, expanding 5.3 per cent in the third quarter of 2026, according to advance estimates.
Some economists believe this gives Bank Negara room to "normalise" interest rates by returning the OPR to its previous level.
What would a rate hike mean for your loans?
For homeowners with floating-rate mortgages, a 25-basis-point increase would generally mean higher monthly repayments.
For example, a RM300,000 outstanding housing loan with 25 years remaining and an effective interest rate of four per cent would carry monthly repayments of about RM1,584.
If the rate increases to 4.25 per cent, repayments could rise to approximately RM1,625, or RM41 more a month.
For a RM500,000 loan under the same conditions, the increase would be around RM68 a month.
These are illustrative calculations. Actual repayments depend on individual loan terms and banks' adjustments.
What about car loans and savings?
Existing fixed-rate car loans generally would not be affected, although variable-rate financing could become more expensive.
Credit card interest rates also do not automatically increase when the OPR rises.
Savers, meanwhile, could benefit from better fixed deposit returns if banks adjust their deposit rates upwards.
Will Bank Negara actually raise rates?
The majority of economists expect the central bank to hold off for now, particularly with inflation remaining manageable at 1.8 per cent in September.
Others argue that stronger growth warrants a return to three per cent to prevent borrowing costs from remaining unnecessarily low.
The debate comes as several central banks, including those in the UK and Japan, have raised interest rates this year amid renewed inflation pressures.
For Malaysia, however, the question is whether stronger growth alone is sufficient reason to reverse last year's precautionary cut.
Bank Negara's decision at 3pm could provide an important indication of where borrowing costs are headed in 2027.

9377170f8571f0e6: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump's stunning midterm defeat by the Democrats has upended another US election — the race to replace him in the White House in 2028.
The crushing defeat for the Republicans is particularly stinging for Vice-President JD Vance, who had been the frontrunner but now risks being seen as tied to his lame-duck boss.
But the midterms are a potential launchpad for rising Democratic stars such as Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, whose youthful appeal has already drawn comparisons with former president Barack Obama.
Republicans in turmoil
The MAGA coalition that propelled Trump to power in 2016 and 2024 effectively collapsed in Tuesday's midterms, leaving any presumptive Republican heir with a mountain to climb.

Long seen as the odds-on favourite for the Republican nomination in 2028, Vance is the most obvious victim after hitching his wagon to Trump throughout the midterm campaign, attending rallies in swing states.
The ambitious 42-year-old quickly tried to distance himself from the electoral disaster, blaming it on Trump's unpopular war on Iran in a lengthy post on X on Wednesday.
But voters are likely to reject his attempts to disown Trump.

It is a familiar problem for US vice-presidents. Former Democratic candidate and vice-president Kamala Harris faced a similar problem in 2024 when she said that "there's not a thing that comes to mind" when asked how she would differentiate herself from Joe Biden.
"The bad news for Vance is that sitting vice-presidents seldom win the presidency," James Lindsay of the Council on Foreign Relations said.
Trump's Secretary of State Marco Rubio's name has also been bandied about.
Rubio, 55, has kept a far lower profile during the midterms, but any top official in Trump's administration will struggle to wash their hands of the Iran war.
The Republicans' midterm disaster could, however, boost other possible candidates.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, 48, who ran against Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, has suddenly become very vocal.
He described the Democratic sweep as "the political equivalent of a meteor strike" and pointed out that it was only in his own state that Republicans held them off.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz, 55, has also left the door open, having run against Trump in 2016 — although his chances may have been harmed by the Democrats' stunning Senate and gubernatorial victories in his state in the midterms.
Democrats on a high
The Democratic field is crowded, but the midterms have given some likely candidates a boost.
Ossoff's re-election as a Georgia senator has fuelled speculation about a 2028 run by the telegenic politician, who has already gained attention for mocking Trump's relationship with a young staffer.
The 39-year-old has said that he has "zero interest in running for president", but his swiftly declared victory in Georgia — and his victory speech — have bolstered his standing in the party.
Before the midterms, Kamala Harris, 62, had been the favourite for the nomination, but many in the party would prefer someone without a losing track record.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, 53, who was interviewed by Harris to be her running mate in 2024, had a good night on Tuesday as he stormed to re-election in the key battleground state.

Outgoing California Governor Gavin Newsom, 59, is another big name who has repeatedly taken on Trump. In an interview with AFP in September, he predicted that Trump's presidency "as we know it would be over after the midterms".
But Newsom, like Harris, may be seen as more of an old-guard figure in a party that is looking to its rising stars.

A prominent but potentially divisive choice would be left-wing New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who said in September that she was weighing a run, musing about whether a Latina could win in a country that rejected female nominees in 2016 and 2024.

Other possible contenders include former Chicago mayor Rahm Emanuel, JB Pritzker, the billionaire Illinois governor who set out a lengthy national agenda after winning a third term on Tuesday, Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, and Arizona Senator and former astronaut Mark Kelly.

c05c49afb7ef3a03: PARIS: The cooling system of France's blood bank has been hit by a cyberattack similar to the hacker attack targeting refrigeration systems across Europe earlier this week, the EFS bank said on Wednesday, reported German Press Agency (dpa).
Cooling rooms at three of the bank's locations have been affected, EFS said.
The refrigeration systems, supplied by an external provider, were manipulated remotely, causing operating temperatures to rise to very high levels, it said.
Temperatures rose from -30°C to 11°C, according to investigative newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné.
Thanks to monitoring and alarm systems, the rise in temperature was detected quickly and action was taken swiftly. No samples or blood products were compromised, according to EFS.
The affected systems have since been brought under control, and blood products have been transferred to other facilities as a precautionary measure, it said.
EFS stores blood products and biological samples in cooling units before they are delivered to healthcare facilities.

The incident comes after cybercriminals targeted fridges and freezers in European supermarkets, causing temperatures to rise, including in Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, Luxembourg, Estonia, Finland, Germany and the Netherlands.
A similar large-scale attack in mid-October caused fridges to warm up in major French supermarket chains.
It remains unclear who was behind the attacks.
9ac961ed71311970: Google-owned autonomous cab company Waymo has revealed it will stop allowing Uber users to book its robo-cabs, hours before the OG rideshare giant made a case for all autonomous vehicle fleet operators to use its platform instead of creating their own.

This slow-motion fender bender played out across Wednesday, starting with Waymo Co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana telling Bloomberg that her company would end a partnership that saw it work exclusively with Uber in Austin and Atlanta.
Mawakana said Waymo wasn’t happy about the fact that when users of Uber’s app requested a ride in one of its robo-cabs, they weren’t guaranteed to get one.

News of that break-up came on the same day that Uber announced its quarterly results. As is common on such occasions, the company published remarks [PDF] its execs intend to make during an earnings call.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi used those remarks to promote the idea that Uber is the natural home for robotaxi fleet operators, because it already delivers around 30 percent higher trips per vehicle per day compared to apps run by autonomous cab companies. He said that higher utilization rate, plus use of shared charging and maintenance infrastructure, can deliver “higher fleet profitability even after paying Uber’s marketplace fee.”

“As autonomous technology becomes more widely available, we believe this ability to commercialize vehicles profitably will become an increasingly important source of competitive advantage and value capture.”

The two events are deliciously ironic, because Uber is arguing the scale of its platform makes it the ideal host for third-party players – just as Google does with its search, app store, and YouTube services. Left unsaid is that the two companies hold concerningly dominant positions in their respective markets.

Khosrowshahi also outlined more ways Uber intends to strengthen its position, including by putting around 2,000 robo-cabs on the road in 2027, before “a much larger commercial ramp beginning in 2028.” That plan means Uber will run some cars itself and rely on third-party robo-cab operators who allow bookings on its app.

“Importantly, building a broad ecosystem does not mean spreading our resources evenly,” the CEO explained. “We intend to maintain an open platform while concentrating capital, integration resources, and hands-on deployment support behind a smaller group of partners with the clearest paths to commercial scale and attractive economics at maturity.”
Or in other words, as Uber uses more robo-cabs, it will try to maximize profits.
Uber users booked $59.8 billion worth of services in its third quarter, up 20 percent year-over-year. The company recognized $14.75 billion of that as revenue, a ten percent improvement.
Rideshare accounted for $29.5 billion of bookings and $7.5 billion of revenue. Delivery services brought in $5.5 billion of revenue on $28.5 billion of bookings.
No wonder Khosrowshahi wants more robo-cabs: they’ll boost Uber’s more lucrative business.

The company might need that boost because Australia’s High Court yesterday decided [PDF] that the company must pay AU$81 million ($57 million) in State payroll taxes because the fees paid to rideshare drivers are effectively wages. While the case considered Uber’s activities in one of Australia’s six States, all of them charge payroll tax. The case is one of many around the world in which courts have found gig workers should be treated as employees for legal and tax purposes. The High Court is Australia’s highest judicial authority and like-minded jurisdictions around the world are aware of its decisions, potentially making more trouble for Uber further down the road. ®
