10c9c28c3bdd4259: <!--kg-card-end: html--> It’s a small pleasure, but receiving an “I Voted” sticker after casting my ballot is one of my favorite parts of the whole voting process. I slap the sticker on my chest and spend the rest of the day feeling like I accomplished a little something. I participated in democracy and everyone who sees me will know it. Artificial intelligence robbed me of that small joy this year and replaced it with a small horror. My “I Voted” sticker is AI-generated slop.

Getting a little sticker when you vote has been a tradition in the US since the 1980s. It’s a symbol of the election cycle. People take selfies and post them or share them with friends. It’s a celebration of democracy and a small way to pressure people into going to the ballot box.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The voting sticker has been subject to every kind of discourse imaginable. Are “I Voted” stickers worth the cost? Wondered Marketplace in 2020. A cemetery in New York has spent time and money tending to the grave of Susan B Anthony because voters coat it in stickers during voting season. In 2008, companies like Starbucks and Ben and Jerry’s ran afoul of election laws for offering free treats to people who showed their “I Voted” stickers.
It’s appropriate but depressing that I got an AI slop “I Voted” sticker in 2026, the year it feels like the mainstream began to reckon with AI.

My sticker is ugly. It’s a busy circular nightmare. “I Voted” is spelled out in small bronze text at the top of the ring. Bronze laurels encircle a bronze bald eagle that stretches atop the American flag. Below this is more text: “250 YEARS ANNIVERSARY” and "SEMIQUENCENTENNIAL.” Below that, another line reads — as best I can tell — “CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA.” I assume this was meant to say “CELEBRATING FREEDOM," but whoever churned out this slop wasn’t using the latest models and the fine detail is lost.

I put the sticker on reluctantly, but I was not proud. I sent a photo of the offending sticker to journalist friends with my face cropped out. They immediately noticed it was AI-generated. I did not post my sticker online. I shared it with no one else. My democratic joy turned to shame.

A few hours later, a friend sent me a selfie. He’d just left the voting booth. His sticker was beautiful, tasteful, a testament to the subtle art of the “I Voted” sticker. A red ring enclosed a blue field. The crescent and palmetto (symbols of South Carolina) sat elegantly behind a bold white “I VOTED.”

His sticker catches the eye. Passers-by will know exactly what the sticker says. They know he voted. Anyone looking at my sticker will wonder how I spilled some bronze paint on my chest. I trembled with indignation. One town over from me they’re giving out the good stickers and I’m stuck with slop. First my town of 12,000 installs 33 Flock cameras and now this?

I spent some time scrolling through social media to see other “I Voted” stickers. So many are so beautiful. Michigan runs a contest where students can submit their own idea for a sticker and the state will print up the winners. Kentucky, Albany, and several other places around the country do the same. Louisiana commissions local artists to produce gorgeous stickers. My mouth hung up in a jealous scowl as I stared at pictures of New Orleanians bedecked with a sticker showing a hand drawn trumpet blasting out “I Voted” alongside Mardi Gras beads.

Only Denton, Texas (another place I’ve lived, weirdly) seems to also have AI-generated slop stickers. Denton’s sticker is, at least, personalized. The city’s court house is in the corner looking more or less correct. The “I Voted” is large and centered in the sticker itself. Like mine, the image is too busy. Too much text, too many fireworks, and the inclusion of the Liberty Bell clutters the whole thing up. The central message — “I Voted” — is bright white. It doesn’t sink into a busy bronze soup like on my sticker.

Complaining about AI-slop “I Voted” stickers may seem trivial in a world where AIs are choosing targets in warzones and vibecoders are reverse-engineering every piece of software ever written. But these little things are important. These small annoyances pile up until things like ChatGPT flyers are so ubiquitous that you don’t notice them anymore. The AI drive-thru works well enough and one day you stop worrying about it so much. You get an ugly AI slop “I Voted” sticker and you slap it on or toss it out. Enough of these build up until you don’t notice that AI all around you. And then, one day, it’s all normal.

Right now we’re figuring out where our AI lines are. Society is negotiating what the future will look like. We’re fighting data centers, figuring out how to burn tokens to keep our bosses happy, and learning what we will and won’t abide.
Me? I draw the line at AI-generated “I Voted” stickers.
570887b3be63b924: Achille with Patroclo. Andre B da Cruz UNIPI, CC BYOn an Ethiopian plateau, a bull called Achille formed an unusual relationship with a male donkey named Patroclo. They were observed spending time together, licking and rubbing against one another, and repeatedly having penetrative sex. The animals’ names nod to Achilles and Patroclus, the Greek mythological figures whose bond has been debated for thousands of years: devoted friends – or lovers? A new study in the journal Current Biology asks something similar about Achille and Patroclo: why would two males of different species repeatedly choose each other as sexual partners when females of their own species are available? Perhaps the more interesting question is why we find their relationship so surprising. A chance find The researchers first noticed Achille and Patroclo while studying gelada monkeys in Ethiopia. Intrigued, they began observing the pair more closely. They recorded 51 mounting attempts, 34 of which involved penetration. Patroclo took an active role, presenting his hindquarters to Achille and initiating contact. Unlike another male donkey that Achille approached, Patroclo did not show obvious signs of trying to avoid him. The donkey and bull often showed affection towards each other immediately after mounting. This suggests that sex may help strengthen their bond. The researchers observed the pair in detail for just four days, so they cannot say how long the relationship lasted. Even so, the findings are unusual because the two animals are both male and belong to different species. Same-sex sexual behaviour has been reported in more than 1,500 animal species. A 2023 study documented it in 261 mammalian species and found that it was particularly associated with social species, suggesting a possible role in maintaining relationships and managing conflict. As a primatologist, I am not surprised by these findings. Bonobos, for example, are famous for their frequent sexual interactions, which occur in many combinations of partners. Female–female genital rubbing, for instance, is associated with affiliation and social bonding. Sexual interactions can also help manage social tensions. Same-sex sexual behaviour takes many forms. Male bottlenose dolphins mount one another and rub genitals in groups that cooperate to gain access to females, while female Japanese macaques form temporary sexual partnerships involving repeated mounting. Same-sex sexual behaviour may play a part in establishing status, settling disputes, forming friendships or sexual enjoyment. Sexual behaviour between different species is rarer, but it is not unheard of. Both male and female Japanese macaques, for example, mount sika deer. Unlike the apparently reciprocal relationship between Achille and Patroclo, these encounters do not necessarily involve mutual sexual interest. What makes Achille and Patroclo particularly interesting is that they combine sexual activity with apparent affection and a preference for each other. Evolutionary biologists have traditionally approached same-sex sexual behaviour as a puzzle. If natural selection favours traits that contribute to reproductive success, why should animals spend time and energy engaging in sexual behaviour that cannot directly produce offspring? Suggested explanations include mistaken identity, a lack of opposite-sex partners, or indiscriminate sexual behaviour with whichever individuals happen to be nearby. But all these explanations begin with an assumption that sexual behaviour between males and females is the default, and same-sex behaviour represents a departure from it. In a provocative 2019 paper, a team of researchers challenged this assumption. They proposed that the ancestors of sexually reproducing animals may have been relatively indiscriminate about the sex of their sexual partners. Rather than assuming that different-sex sexual behaviour came first, they suggested that the ability to distinguish between potential partners, and preferentially direct sexual behaviour towards the opposite sex, may have evolved later. Taking a queer perspective This is a brilliant example of how queer perspectives can enrich evolutionary biology. Queer approaches encourage scientists to examine how human assumptions about sex, gender and sexuality influence the questions we ask, the categories we use and the explanations we consider plausible. They do not require us to assign human sexual identities to animals. Observing same-sex sexual behaviour does not tell us that an animal is gay or establish a fixed sexual orientation. Instead, queer approaches encourage us to take the diversity of animal sexual behaviour seriously, without assuming what is normal or what needs explaining. The authors of the new study suggest that Achille and Patroclo’s sexual interactions may help maintain their social relationship. They also discuss the possible reproductive costs of spending time and energy on sexual activity that cannot result in offspring. But this framing raises another question. Why should we assume that sexual behaviour must contribute directly to reproduction to have evolutionary significance? Social relationships can influence survival, access to resources and future reproductive opportunities. Sexual behaviour that strengthens those relationships may therefore have adaptive benefits, even when it cannot directly produce offspring. Equally, sexual behaviour may arise from evolved mechanisms without every individual encounter necessarily providing an animal’s reproductive success. Achille and Patroclo cannot tell us why they choose one another. This short study can’t tell us what evolutionary purpose, if any, their relationship serves. But it does remind us that animal behaviour can be more diverse than our theories suggest. Perhaps the most important lesson is not that a bull and a donkey have formed an unusual sexual relationship. It is that understanding such relationships requires us to question our assumptions about what sex is, what it does, and what counts as natural. Jo Setchell does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
e1e3c8d3dff12e6c: It’s rare to see an executive go from fucking around to finding out so quickly. That’s what happened last week when Proton CEO Andy Yen announced he was canceling a planned re-interview process for almost all current employees that would have checked if they’re using AI enough. This follows extreme backlash from Proton users and workers against the company's aggressive pivot to AI. It’s been a wild ride internally, several employees past and present have shared with 404 Media.

On Friday, Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, cancelled a series of nearly company-wide ‘re-interviews’ that would have forced employees to explain how they are using AI, with the clear intention that they may be fired if not using it enough in the eyes of Proton leadership, according to six current Proton employees and audio of an around two hour all-hands meeting obtained by 404 Media.

The move came after 404 Media published an investigation on Thursday, which showed how Yen was aggressively pushing AI across Proton, in some cases despite security concerns from employees. In one exchange, an employee in the company’s security Slack channel urged Proton to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” Yen added, “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

The re-interview cancellations likely don’t address the concerns of many Proton users, who are more focused on Proton’s deprioritization of security; many Proton users have blasted the company’s leadership on social media over the last 24 hours and explicitly called for Yen to resign.

Kinktober has come and gone. But Archive of Our Own (AO3), a massive repository for fanfiction and creative writing, is still down, and might be down for as long as a month after going down for "maintenance" following a security incident last week. The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted on its status page that the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month.

People are coping how they can. And they’re turning to anything but Wattpad to fill the void. One writer I spoke to who posts her writing and reads others’ writing on AO3 told me that she was in the middle of racing to finish a work that was deliberately timed to Kinktober and Halloween when the outage happened. She was hitting “next chapter” while reading a fic on Wednesday night when she got the message that the site was down for maintenance, “which I initially took as a sign from the universe to go to bed,” she said.

00:10:00 BARRY RITHOLTZ: So that’s in the mid-2010s, somewhere along those lines?
00:10:03 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah, that’s right.

4d3744be4285318b: Does it make sense to wait until late December to wrap up, like these California shoppers did in 2023? Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty ImagesAmazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October. But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping. As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions, I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping. Why retailers get such an early start Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S. Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey. But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween. Some do this out of necessity: They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks. For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually. In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping. Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds. And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season. A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics, since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs. Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October. Early birds could buy these Christmas decorations at a discount on Oct. 17, 2026. Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies. Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees. In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1. Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas. The timing of holiday shopping varies whether you buy gifts online or in brick-and-mortar stores. Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images When buying early makes financial sense Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary. For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price. But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out. And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items. Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget, recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping. 6a62b628a03d80c8: From Ashraf Abdullah
Moaz Nair’s “Bedfellows and backstabbers on the winding road to Putrajaya” mistakes colourful language for a convincing explanation of Malaysian politics.

His argument rests on two questionable assumptions: that cooperation in the federal government requires permanent electoral allegiance, and that the next general election is guaranteed to produce a hung Parliament.
Neither should pass unchallenged.
The unity government emerged after GE15 in November 2022, when no coalition secured a parliamentary majority.

The 16th Yang di-Pertuan Agong urged political cooperation to resolve the impasse. Umno’s supreme council subsequently supported its participation in a unity government, specifying that it should not be led by Perikatan Nasional.

That context matters. Barisan Nasional (BN) helped establish a functioning administration following an inconclusive election. It did not merge with Pakatan Harapan (PH) or surrender its political identity.

Supporting an administration during a parliamentary term and deciding whom to contest alongside at the next election are distinct decisions. Describing that distinction as “backstabbing” requires more than metaphors about political bedrooms.

For accuracy, BN’s leadership has previously advocated extending cooperation into GE16. In June 2024, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said BN would maintain cooperation with PH while contesting under its own symbol. That statement cannot simply be erased from the record.
But neither can it be treated as an irrevocable undertaking regardless of subsequent developments.
In January this year, Umno secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said the party had not decided whether cooperation with PH would continue at GE16.

More recently, Zahid reaffirmed BN’s commitment to the unity government until the end of the present Parliament. These statements underline why the governing commitment, and future electoral arrangements must be examined separately.

Zahid’s preference alone should not determine BN’s electoral future. As Umno president and BN chairman, he must secure support within his party and take into account the positions of other BN component parties.

Umno members, its decision-making bodies, MCA and MIC have interests and constituencies of their own. An arrangement affecting their survival requires collective backing. Leadership involves listening to those whom one leads. And lest we forget, BN makes decisions by consensus.
It must also involve listening to voters.
In my assessment, continued electoral cooperation with PH will be increasingly difficult to sell to voters frustrated by promises which remain unfulfilled.
PH campaigned on reform and better governance. Its supporters are entitled to judge the delivery against the expectations its leaders created.

BN cannot assume that those frustrations are somebody else’s problem. Sharing power also means sharing public scrutiny. Ignoring discontent to preserve an understanding between leaders could prove costly at the ballot box.

Resistance among many Malay voters to cooperation with DAP presents another challenge. This does not mean every Malay voter thinks alike, or that election results establish a single reason for voting.
They do, however, require BN to examine whether its present partnership helps recover traditional supporters or pushes them further away.

Nair’s treatment of Umno and PAS is heavy with derision. I find considerable venom in his descriptions of Umno and PAS in this particular article and in his past jottings, perhaps because both are Malay-based parties.
He makes little effort to understand the constituencies these parties represent. Their supporters deserve analysis rather than caricature.
The election evidence also deserves more attention than his confident prediction allows.

In Sabah’s November 2025 election, DAP failed to win any of the eight seats it contested. Its secretary-general Loke Siew Fook accepted responsibility. Much of the electoral benefit went to Warisan, illustrating that dissatisfaction with DAP need not translate automatically into support for MCA.
Nevertheless, the warning was unmistakable: established support cannot be taken for granted.
Johor delivered another forceful reminder. In the July 2026 state election, BN won 48 of 56 seats, including eight won by MCA. PH secured eight seats, six through DAP. PN failed to win a seat.
Those results demonstrate both BN’s renewed strength and the danger of assuming that any party possesses an unassailable electoral base.

An analysis by the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, part of Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore identified declining Chinese support for PH alongside weaker turnout in its urban strongholds.
Its estimates still placed most Chinese voters with PH but showed meaningful erosion. A party need not lose an entire community’s support to lose constituencies where the contest is close.
Some voters may choose MCA. Others may abstain. Neither response guarantees a particular national outcome, but both can alter electoral arithmetic.

Negeri Sembilan offers a different, equally relevant lesson. BN won 18 seats, PN seven and PH 11 in its August election. BN and PN therefore held 25 of the assembly’s 36 seats between them. Cooperation mattered to the resulting balance of power.

It would nevertheless be inaccurate to describe that result as proof of a wholesale Chinese rejection of PH. Bridget Welsh’s analysis estimated that Chinese support remained overwhelmingly with PH. The stronger argument concerns the combination of constituency results and cooperation between competing political forces.
Together, these elections challenge the notion that PH’s position is secure or that fragmentation must inevitably produce another hung Parliament.
My assessment is that an effective BN-PN electoral understanding could win a comfortable parliamentary majority.
Avoiding mutually damaging contests, consolidating overlapping support and recovering some non-Malay votes offer a credible route to that outcome.

That remains a forecast. Seat negotiations, candidates, turnout and the positions of Sabah and Sarawak parties will matter. But Nair cannot reasonably demand certainty from competing scenarios while presenting his own as guaranteed.

He should visit Melaka and take the pulse of the campaign. BN is contesting 23 seats and PN five. Zahid has publicly said BN would invite successful PN assemblymen into the administration if it forms the government. This is an openly stated political understanding, not a clandestine affair.
Melaka votes on Nov 14. Its verdict remains with the electorate.
Cooperation in government does not confer permanent ownership over a partner’s electoral choices.
Changed arrangements require explanation, but they do not automatically establish betrayal.
The road to Putrajaya may be winding but a hung Parliament, to my mind, is not a foregone conclusion, like Nair confidently puts it.
The writer is a former group managing editor of Media Prima Bhd’s Television Networks.

624e23d0cdf0ab77: Regina Barzilay, MIT’s School of Engineering Distinguished Professor of AI and Health, and James Collins, MIT’s Termeer Professor of Medical Engineering and Science, are the recipients of the 2026 Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence.  The award recognizes their joint work in “pioneering AI-enabled antibiotic discovery, integrating deep learning, bioengineering, and experimental validation to identify novel antibacterial candidates against drug-resistant pathogens.”  Established in 2024 by the University of Chicago in partnership with Caltech, the Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence recognizes contributions that jointly advance AI and the natural sciences or engineering. Barzilay and Collins, who are faculty co-leads of the Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and affiliates of the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing and the MIT School of Engineering, published their first breakthrough paper together in 2020 with then-MIT postdoc and first author Jonathan Stokes (who worked in the Collins lab from 2017 to 2021) in Cell. The paper described the first artificial intelligence-discovered antibiotic, called halicin, named for the fictional AI system HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey. A broad-spectrum antibiotic that was originally studied as a potential diabetes drug, halicin was identified by a deep learning model trained on 2,500 molecules. Upon testing, the research team found that halicin was able to kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria (i.e., “superbugs”) such as Clostridium difficile, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A discovery process that once took years was completed in just a few weeks. Amidst the growing alarm around the global antimicrobial resistance crisis, the results demonstrated that AI could prove to be an effective tool for rapidly identifying new and effective antibiotics. Following halicin, Barzilay and Collins worked with Stokes (now an assistant professor at McMaster University) to use machine learning to identify abaucin in 2023, a narrow-spectrum antibiotic demonstrating effectiveness against A. baumannii, an antibiotic-resistant bacteria commonly found on hospital doorknobs and in the wounds of U.S. soldiers stationed in Iraq and Afghanistan. Notably, abaucin’s “narrow spectrum” efficacy against a single species of treatment-resistant bacteria is its main advantage, minimizing the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance and harming beneficial bacteria in the gut. “Historically, antibiotic discovery has depended on laborious, trial-and-error strategies,” says Collins. “This process is slow, costly, and unpredictable, often yielding few viable antibiotic candidates. With generative AI, we're now seeing a shift from AI being used as a tool for discovery to AI being used as a design tool. This shift opens new frontiers in antibiotic discovery that could bring us the next generation of lifesaving drugs.” In Barzilay’s view, “despite significant progress in molecular modeling, we are still in early stages of drug discovery. With AI, we can only automate parts of the pipeline, rather than totally transforming the discovery process. To make it happen, we need to work really hard to build realistic AI models of human biology.”

7feeedd4d2bf32cd: From Moaz Nair
Welcome to the era of "polytropous" politics, a term analysts use when they want to politely say our politicians suffer from severe relationship commitment issues.

As we barrel towards the 16th general election, the political landscape in the Peninsula resembles less a stable Westminster democracy and more a chaotic, high-stakes episode of "The Bachelor: Putrajaya Edition".
For those trying to keep track of the prospective political mathematics, the current options on Anwar Ibrahim’s whiteboard read like labels on a broken calculator:
Pakatan Harapan Plus, Perikatan Nasional Plus, or perhaps a convoluted equation like Barisan Nasional-minus-Bersatu, Wawasan, Gerakan, Malaysian Indian People’s Party, and Pejuang, multiplied by PAS.
The truth is, no one has locked in a mega-coalition because everyone is too busy playing the field.

Take Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, the grand master of political gymnastics. At the federal level, the Umno president sits snugly in the marital bed of the unity government with PH and the DAP, smiling warmly for the cameras.
But the moment he crosses state borders into Johor, Negeri Sembilan, or the electoral war zone of Melaka, Zahid sneaks out the back window to hook up with Abdul Hadi Awang and PAS.
Talk about a shameless double life. Zahid and Anwar run the country together during the week, but come the weekend, BN teams up with PAS to try and wipe PH off the state map.

When launching the Melaka election machinery, Zahid proudly declared that "hijau sudah menerima biru" (green has accepted blue). Yet the irony is loud: BN aggressively kept 23 seats for itself, dumping the remaining five hard-to-win seats on PAS and its PN allies.
But let’s be real — this romance has a strict ceiling.

Zahid wants PAS and PAS only, completely blanking other PN roommates. Besides, is Hadi really going to hand over safe seats in Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah, or Perlis just to be nice to Umno? Local warlords say there's a better chance of snow hitting these states, especially after Umno just squeezed their allies out of two extra seats in Melaka.
PN is trapped

Meanwhile, PN is trapped in a dilemma of its own making. To properly court BN, they are being asked to dump their entire entourage — Gerakan, MIPP, Pejuang, and the newly minted Wawasan led by the exiled Hamzah Zainudin. It turns out Zahid doesn't want to pay for a group dinner.
To make matters funnier, the house that Gerakan and MIPP are clinging to is literally on fire.

In a massive political shockwave on Oct 20, the Registrar of Societies officially cancelled Perikatan Nasional's registration. This stemmed from a toxic internal feud where Bersatu complained it was unlawfully excluded from a crucial PN council meeting. Though the High Court granted a temporary stay on Oct 22, the alliance is legally a "ghost ship" caught in intense friction, while its internal engine — Bersatu under Muhyiddin Yassin — is causing an absolute earthquake of instability.

Naturally, the vacuum has sparked wild rumours. Whisper it, in Shah Alam, but word on the street is that a fractured Bersatu is looking to jump ship entirely and work with PH, starting with a cosy trial marriage in Selangor that could spread nationwide.

This comes hot on the heels of party leaders executing a federal confidence and supply agreement with Anwar Ibrahim’s government — a pact explicitly designed to buy parliamentary stability and secure the passage of the 2027 budget.
If you're keeping score: Zahid is sleeping with PN's partner, while Muhyiddin's remnants are trying to move in with Zahid's federal spouse.

While the Peninsula fractures into a million messy social media threads, East Malaysia is watching the soap opera with mild amusement. The regional titans, Gabungan Parti Sarawak and Gabungan Rakyat Sabah have zero interest in joining a rigid, peninsula-centric bloc or any stressful mega-coalition.
Why buy into the drama now when you can just sit back, secure your own backyard, and wait to play kingmaker after the election?
It's complicated

When the dust settles on GE16, the only guaranteed result is of a spectacularly hung parliament. None of the party leaders, Anwar, Zahid, Muhyiddin, and Hadi, will have the 112-seat magic number to form a government on their own. We won't see clean "plus" coalitions on the ballot paper.

Instead, we will get "fluid understandings"— the political equivalent of "it's complicated". Our leaders will avoid three-cornered fights where convenient, stab each other in the back where necessary, and then awkwardly gather in a hotel ballroom post-election to figure out who hates each other the least.
Brace yourselves. The road to Putrajaya is no longer a highway; it’s a swinging party, and everyone is invited.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

8d8227e52875b593: In 1968, Stanford biologist Paul Ehrlich opened his book The Population Bomb with a sentence that still makes me wince: "The battle to feed all of humanity is over." In the 1970s, he predicted, "hundreds of millions of people will starve to death", no matter what crash programmes we launched.

Instead came the Green Revolution, and between 1960 and 2005 the yields of major cereal crops more than doubled while real food prices fell by over 50%. Yet when a New York Times documentary series asked him about the book in 2015, Ehrlich, who died in March at 93, replied: "My language would be even more apocalyptic today."

I can't help but feel we are watching the same film again, except that this time the bomb is AI. And here's the kicker: the people who understand it best are far less frightened of it than the rest of us.

When the Pew Research Center surveyed Americans in 2024, 51% said they were more concerned than excited about AI, against a mere 15% of the 1,013 AI experts it polled. More than half of those experts, 56%, expected AI to have a positive impact on the United States over the next 20 years, compared with just 17% of the public.

Malaysians, refreshingly, haven't quite caught the bug. In market research firm Ipsos' 2025 survey of 30 countries, 77% of us said AI excites us, the third highest of the lot, though 55% admitted it also makes us nervous.

Now, I'm no doe-eyed optimist. In July, during an internal hacking test, roughly 700 of OpenAI's AI agents found exposed login credentials and broke into the servers of Hugging Face, an outside AI hosting company, and investigators found that the agents knew "this activity was out of scope and unethical", but joined in anyway.

Closer to home, by August 2024 the police's Commercial Crime Investigation Department was already probing 454 scams believed to involve deepfakes, AI-generated fake voices and videos, with RM2.72 million lost. And 63% of Malaysians worry that AI could take their job within the next three to five years.
These are grave dangers, which is exactly why we must build the brakes as we go. But a danger is not a destiny, and the odds, according to the researchers building this technology, are in our favour.

In a survey conducted in late 2023, 2,778 researchers who had published at top AI conferences and journals put the median chance of an extremely bad outcome, such as human extinction, at 5%. That's not nothing, but 68.3% of them said good outcomes were more likely than bad ones.
So what does the good outcome look like? We don't have to imagine it, because much of it is already here:
● Google DeepMind's AlphaFold mapped over 200 million protein shapes, earning its creators a Nobel Prize;
● AI-assisted screening of Swedish women caught 29% more breast cancers, with 44% less radiologist work;
● An AI at University of California San Diego cut hospital sepsis deaths by 17%; and
● A generative AI assistant lifted customer support productivity by 14%, and that of novice workers by 34%

That last point matters to anyone worried about their job, because the tool helped the least experienced workers the most, narrowing the gap between the rookie and the veteran rather than widening it. Just this week, Microsoft said its diagnostic AI correctly diagnosed 83% of complex medical cases against 36% for generalist doctors in a study published in the journal Science, though it has yet to be tested against specialists or on real patients.

And it's already at work in our own public health system. Dr Mata, an AI developed by the Ministry of Health with private firm Qmed Asia, screens diabetics for retinopathy, a leading cause of preventable blindness here, in about 30 seconds, in a country where 15.6% of adults have type 2 diabetes.

Meanwhile, seven government clinics, from Kajang in Selangor to Kok Lanas in Kelantan, were picked last year to pilot AI-assisted chest X-rays designed to catch lung disease earlier, at a one-off software cost of about RM10,000 per clinic.

Where does it go from here? Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who runs Google DeepMind, told CBS's 60 Minutes last year that ending all disease is "within reach. Maybe within the next decade or so, I don't see why not", before asking in the same interview: "Can we make sure that we can keep control of the systems?"
That is precisely the right posture, eyes wide open to the risks but feet firmly moving towards the reward. Fear has its uses, but it makes a terrible driver.

So by all means build the brakes, fund the police's deepfake hunters and retrain the workers whose jobs will change. But the next time someone tells you the battle for humanity's future is already lost, remember the global famine that never came, and the AI our own health ministry helped build that can now screen a diabetic's eyes in 30 seconds.

692b90b8c7c21a69: In every culture, humans speak and sing to each other. We have created an astounding array of languages and musical structures across the globe. And yet, within this diversity, some fundamental sequence patterns are repeated. These are often referred to as “universal” patterns in human vocalization. Our new research, published this week in Science, reveals that many of these acoustic patterns in human song and speech are also shared with birdsong. The study compared the songs of 367 bird species with examples of song and speech from 52 human languages. How we gathered the data As researchers in animal behaviour and neuroscience and music, we (Logan and Jon) spent 10 years documenting the prevalence of universal human acoustic patterns in the songs of zebra finches. A zebra finch. (Unsplash/Angelo Casto) When Kendra joined our lab during her PhD, she proposed we investigate whether these patterns are shared across other bird species as well. To research this, we needed a large number of birdsong recordings. Luckily, many people around the world are fascinated by the sounds of birds and upload their recordings to public repositories. We collected and manually annotated individual syllables in the songs of over 360 bird species, generating more than 70,000 birdsong syllables for analysis. We then compared these to data sets of human speech and song from a variety of languages and cultures around the world. Fortunately, some of these data sets contain annotated recordings of the same individual producing both speech and song, which was perfect for our comparisons to bird vocalizations. Humans and birds both tend to end their phrases with longer syllable. (Unsplash) Regular and predictable rhythms Overall, we found numerous similarities in the acoustic patterns of bird songs and human vocalizations. For example, humans and birds both tend to end their phrases with longer syllables. Song of a fox sparrow. (Patrik Aberg), CC BY-NC-SA35 KB (download) They also organize their syllables in a way that minimizes changes of pitch across adjacent syllables. And they tend to produce their songs with regular and predictable rhythms. In some cases, birdsong appeared more similar to human song than human speech. In other cases, we found birds tended to have songs that were more similar to human speech than human song. Unrelated to vocal learning We designed this study to ask an important question: Does vocal learning ability shape sequence patterning? Humans learn the structure of their vocalizations from others, particularly as they grow up. It turns out many birds also learn their vocalizations as they grow up. We looked at two separate groups of these vocal learning birds: songbirds (oscines) and hummingbirds. We compared them to two closely related bird groups that are not vocal learners: suboscines and nightjars. Because humans, songbirds and hummingbirds are all vocal learners, we thought some patterns may be similar within these species and distinct from those within suboscines and nightjars. Surprisingly, we found very little evidence for this. The degree of variation across bird species did not appear to be related to vocal learning. Yellow-rumped warbler, an oscine songbird. (Unsplash) How humans and birds make sound What then might drive the similarities in sequence patterning across so many species? We will need more studies to determine the answer, but we hypothesize that similarities in how humans and birds produce sounds could shape some vocal sequence patterns. For example, the shared need to co-ordinate breathing with vocal musculature could contribute to shared acoustic patterning across birds and humans. Specifically, precise movement of muscles that control the vocal tract are timed with airflow from the lungs across all birds and humans. If this is true, it’s possible these patterns may be found in many other species. Did birds teach us to sing? Did birdsong influence the evolution of human sound? (Unsplash) Songbirds first evolved about 50 million years ago, long before the first lines of humans split from the other great apes. This means that birds have decorated our soundscapes throughout human evolution. The songs of birds have inspired music throughout time and cultures. Might these natural sounds have influenced the earliest humans as they began experimenting with making sounds themselves, discovering the joy of music to their ears? These are some of the big ideas we are excited to explore in future studies. Logan S. James receives funding from FRQNT. He is affiliated with Earth Species Project and Wavelength Science. Jon Sakata receives funding from NSERC, CIHR, and FRQNT. Kendra Oudyk currently receives funding from SSHRC and formerly received funding from FRQNT while working on this project.
c4847b9309dd62fe: Their most pressing challenge is solving the long-standing water shortage in the village
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the project in Qyzylsay, Kazakhstan. Photo by Nazgul Aidabossynova. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Women in the rural areas of Kazakhstan are among those most affected by climate change, energy deficit, and poor governance. They bear the heavy burden of water shortages, especially in the southern parts of the country, where this problem is the most acute due to dense population, economic reliance on agriculture, and water losses related to outdated irrigation infrastructure.

In the village of Qyzylsay, located in the southern Jambyl region, the water shortage has become a major issue affecting the daily lives of women. It forces them to spend multiple hours a day outside their homes to secure water for their households, gardens, and animals. Their grueling work often goes unnoticed and unpaid, and their geographical remoteness places limits on access to information and government services, exacerbating their situation.

In 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, a local activist, implemented a project to help local women improve their livelihoods by training them to engage with the government more effectively and efficiently, calculate the cost of their labor and products, and mobilize collective efforts to solve community problems. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Aidabossynova to learn more about her initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Nazgul Aidabossynova (NA): I represent a community-based initiative led by rural women in Qyzylsay. Our work focuses on supporting women who manage households, small farms, livestock, and care responsibilities, while also facing limited access to information, public services, and opportunities for civic participation.

We chose to participate in the Digital Sparks project because digital tools can make a direct, practical difference in women’s daily lives. Many women already own smartphones, but previously used them mainly for calls and WhatsApp.

The project created an opportunity to turn these devices into tools for accessing eGov services, documenting community problems, managing farm and household responsibilities, protecting digital security, and communicating with local authorities.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

NA: The key challenge is unreliable access to water in Qyzylsay. Water often disappears from the pipes during the day, particularly in summer. This affects gardens, livestock, household work, and the health and well-being of families.

The burden falls disproportionately on women. They wake early to store water, carry water for household and agricultural needs, care for the livestock, and wait for irrigation turns. Much of this work is unpaid, time-consuming, and rarely recognized.

Women also faced barriers in reporting water problems: they knew what was happening, but often lacked the knowledge, evidence, and confidence needed to raise concerns effectively with local institutions.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
NA: The project delivered four practical training sessions for ten rural women.

The first one, titled “Your Phone is More Than WhatsApp: Smartphone as Your Household Assistant”, taught them how to use smartphone reminders, photo-diaries for farm and livestock work, eGov services, strong passwords, and basic digital-security practices.

In the second workshop, titled “Smart Water: When Your Garden Tells You It’s Thirsty”, participants learned about water rights, the responsibilities of relevant local authorities, and water-supply mapping using timestamped and GPS-tagged photographs.

The third session, titled “Numbers Don’t Lie: When You Count Everything, You Earn More”, covered how to track unpaid work and calculate the real cost of agricultural products such as milk. It also discussed the economic value of time saved through smart irrigation.

In “Honest Agreement: When Technology Helps Us Trust Each Other”, the fourth and final session, participants prepared time-to-income plans, mapped local support networks, discussed peer mentoring, and agreed to begin work toward a cooperative approach to water advocacy and shared smart-irrigation infrastructure.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
NA: The project helped participating women see smartphones as tools for independence, civic participation, and practical problem-solving, rather than only communication devices.
For example, women learned that they can use eGov services to request certain official documents online, reducing the need to spend time and money traveling to administrative offices.

They also learned to create structured evidence of water problems. A photograph of a dry canal, broken pipe, or contaminated water source becomes more useful for advocacy when it includes the date, location, and a written description.

The training on unpaid labor and production costs was especially meaningful. Participants calculated the value of their time and better understood the real cost of milk production and irrigation work. The discussion showed that manual irrigation may take up to 60 hours per month.
This helped participants recognize that their time has economic value, and that shared smart-irrigation solutions could create more time for income, education, rest, and community participation.
The group also began a peer-learning process. Three participants started sharing the knowledge gained during the training with neighboring women.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
NA: My understanding of digital democracy has become much more practical. Before this project, digital tools could be viewed mainly as a way to communicate or access information.
Through Digital Sparks, I saw how digital tools can strengthen people’s ability to exercise rights, access public services, collect evidence, engage with local authorities, and organize collectively.
I also gained a stronger understanding of the link between digital inclusion, women’s unpaid labor, climate-related water challenges, and civic space.

For rural women, digital capacity is not only about technical skills. It is about having a voice, being able to document problems, understanding their rights, and participating in decisions that affect their families and community.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

NA: The most valuable lesson is that digital literacy has the greatest impact when it is directly connected to people’s real, daily needs. In Qyzylsay, water shortages, agricultural work, unpaid care responsibilities, and access to public services were the issues that made digital tools relevant and useful.

Another important lesson is that women need not only information, but also confidence and collective support. When participants understood their rights, calculated the value of their labor, and learned how to create reliable evidence, they became more prepared to speak with local authorities and work together.
The project also showed the value of peer learning. Participants are more likely to trust and learn from women in their own community who face similar challenges.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?
NA: We will continue the peer cascade model, with trained participants sharing basic smartphone, eGov, digital safety, and evidence documentation skills with other women in Qyzylsay.

The group intends to develop a cooperative approach to the village’s water challenges. The planned cooperative would support joint advocacy, shared learning, and exploration of funding opportunities for smart-well or shared irrigation infrastructure.

In future work, we will continue combining digital skills with women’s economic empowerment, rights awareness, and local civic participation, so that rural women’s work, knowledge, and needs become more visible.
